content: The FDA has requested that the manufacturer of Hydroxycut remove the product from distribution. This decision was made because Hydroxycut has been linked to cases of liver failure, including one fatality resulting from liver failure. It is hypothesized that hydroxycitric acid, a compound derived from a tropical fruit and included in the product, may be the ingredient associated with these adverse effects. Hydroxycut is marketed as a weight-loss aid, designed to help consumers lose weight by increasing metabolism and reducing hunger cravings. It is sold through major retailers such as GNC and Walmart, as well as via direct television marketing. Currently, Hydroxycut is sold in the United States without ephedra and is advertised as a product that boosts metabolism and suppresses appetite. However, like many nutraceuticals, its efficacy remains questionable. The product is promoted as being developed and endorsed by medical professionals. One of its endorsers is a 2005 graduate of Midwestern University’s medical school, who is still in residency. Another endorser is Marvin Heuer, MD, FAAFP, an Associate Clinical Professor in the Department of Family Medicine and Community Health at the University of Florida. On March 27, 2003, Missouri’s Attorney General, Jay Nixon, filed a lawsuit in St. Louis against Hydroxycut’s manufacturer, MuscleTech Research and Development, Inc. The lawsuit alleged that claims stating Hydroxycut was clinically proven to be a fat-burner were false. Additionally, Nixon accused the company of using misleading before and after photographs in their marketing. One example cited was a before photo of a woman who had recently been pregnant, which was deemed deceptive. MuscleTech ultimately paid $100,000 to settle the case, while denying any wrongdoing.
